questions.title: Entity
questions.text: Which statement best defines an **entity**?

options.content: A single property such as a surname
A thing, person or event about which data is stored
A field that uniquely identifies a record

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: An entity has its own data and many instances; it becomes a table. A single property is an attribute.

questions.title: Attribute
questions.text: *A cinema stores films, screenings and customers.* Which item is an **attribute**, not an entity?

scheme.mark_scheme: D.
scheme.explanation: Running time is one value that describes a film, so it is a field of the Film table.

questions.title: Order of design
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

First the analyst identifies the [[1]] and their attributes from the requirements. Then the relationships are drawn in an [[2]]. Finally every field is described in the data [[3]].

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) entities (2) ERD (3) dictionary

questions.title: Entity or attribute
questions.text:
*A car-rental company records customers, cars and rentals. For each car it stores the registration number, model and daily price.*

Tick (✓) **one** box in each row.

scheme.mark_scheme: Customer entity (1); Daily price attribute (1); Rental entity (1); Model attribute (1)
scheme.model_answer: Customer — entity; Daily price — attribute; Rental — entity; Model — attribute.
scheme.explanation: Customer and Rental have their own data and many instances; daily price and model are single values describing a car.

questions.title: Design documents
questions.text: Match each document or statement to what it contains.

right.text: The design built in the DBMS
The name, type, size, key and validation of every field
The tables and how they are related (1:1, 1:M)
What the client needs the system to store and report

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R4, L2–R3, L3–R2, L4–R1. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Choosing a primary key
questions.text: A music school stores `StudentID`, `FirstName`, `Surname`, `DateOfBirth` and `ParentPhone` for each student. Which field is the most suitable **primary key**?

scheme.mark_scheme: C.
scheme.explanation: A primary key must be unique, never empty and should not change. Surnames and birthdays repeat; a parent's phone can change or be shared by siblings.

questions.title: Degree of a relationship
questions.text: Match each pair of entities to the degree of the relationship between them.

left.text: Country — Capital city (each country has one capital)
Class — Pupil (a pupil is in one class)
Student — Elective course (students take several electives)

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R1, L2–R3, L3–R2. One mark per correct match.
scheme.explanation: Ask the question in both directions: a class has many pupils, but a pupil is in one class → 1:M.

questions.title: Where the foreign key goes
questions.text: One teacher teaches many lessons; each lesson has one teacher. Where is the foreign key `TeacherID` placed?

options.content: In both tables, as a primary key

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: The foreign key goes in the table on the "many" side of a 1:M relationship.

questions.title: Storing M:M
questions.text: A many-to-many relationship can be implemented directly by adding one foreign key to either of the two tables.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: A field holds only one value, so one foreign key cannot list many partners. An M:M relationship is replaced by a link entity with two foreign keys.

questions.title: Name the link entity
questions.text: A school library: each member borrows many books, and each book is borrowed by many members over a year. State a suitable name for the **link entity** that resolves this many-to-many relationship.

scheme.mark_scheme: Loan
scheme.explanation: One record per borrowing — the Loan — holds MemberID and BookID as foreign keys, plus the dates.

questions.title: Degrees in a gym
questions.text:
*A gym: each training session is for one member with one trainer; members have many sessions; trainers run many sessions; a member may train with several trainers.*

Tick (✓) **one** box in each row.

scheme.model_answer: Member — Session — 1:M; Trainer — Session — 1:M; Member — Trainer — M:M.
scheme.explanation: Session is the link entity that resolves Member M:M Trainer into two 1:M relationships.

questions.title: Crow's foot
questions.text: In crow's foot notation, what does the crow's foot (three short lines) at one end of a relationship line show?

options.content: That entity is on the "one" side
That entity is on the "many" side
That entity has no primary key

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: The crow's foot touches the entity that has many records for one record of the other entity.

questions.title: Fields of a link entity
questions.text: The link entity **Loan** resolves Member M:M Book. Select the **three** fields that Loan should contain.

scheme.mark_scheme: A and B and D. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Names and titles are already stored in Member and Book; repeating them in Loan would be redundant.

questions.title: Why design first
questions.text: Select **two** reasons why the database is designed (ERD and data dictionary) **before** the tables are built.

options.content: Errors are found on paper before data is entered
The tables no longer need primary keys
Programmers build tables whose keys and types fit together

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Errors in an ERD
questions.text: A student drew this ERD for a hospital: *Doctor M——M Patient* (no other entities); `DoctorID` is stored as a foreign key in the Doctor table. Select the **two** errors.

options.content: The M:M relationship has not been resolved with a link entity such as Appointment
Doctor and Patient should not be entities
A foreign key is placed in the table where it is the primary key
Crow's foot notation cannot show M:M

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Build an ERD: a gym
questions.text:
A gym keeps data about its **members**, **trainers** and training **sessions**. Each session is for one member with one trainer. A member has many sessions, and a trainer runs many sessions.

Draw the ERD: add one box per entity (its name on the first line), connect the entities that are related, then select each line and choose its degree. Do **not** leave a many-to-many relationship in the diagram. Draw only the entities the scenario needs.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Entities: Member, Trainer, Session (1 item each)
Relationships: Member 1:M Session; Trainer 1:M Session (1 item each, with the correct degree)
5 items in all; the 3 marks are given in proportion to the correct items. Each extra entity or line cancels one correct item.
scheme.model_answer: Member 1 —— M Session M —— 1 Trainer
scheme.explanation: Member and Trainer are M:M; the Session entity resolves it into two 1:M relationships with the crow's feet at Session.

questions.title: Data dictionary
questions.text: Which statement best describes a **data dictionary**?

options.content: The records stored in the database
A diagram of the entities and relationships
A description of every field of every table: name, type, size, key and validation
A list of the users of the system

scheme.mark_scheme: C.
scheme.explanation: A data dictionary holds metadata — data about the data — not the records themselves.

questions.title: Items in a data dictionary
questions.text: Select **three** items recorded in a data dictionary for each field.

options.content: The value typed by the last user

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C and D. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Data types for Rental
questions.text: Complete the data dictionary for the table `Rental` with the most suitable data type. Use **INT**, **VARCHAR**, **DATE**, **DECIMAL**, **BOOLEAN**.

scheme.mark_scheme: RegNo VARCHAR (1); StartDate DATE (1); Days INT (1); Deposit DECIMAL (1)
scheme.model_answer: RegNo VARCHAR; StartDate DATE; Days INT; Deposit DECIMAL.
scheme.explanation: A registration number contains letters; money needs two decimal places.

questions.title: Phone number type
questions.text: Which is the most suitable data type and size for `ParentPhone` with values such as `+77015554433`?

scheme.mark_scheme: C.
scheme.explanation: A phone number begins with + or 0 and is never used in arithmetic, so it is text; 12 characters fit +7 and 10 digits.

questions.title: Money data type
questions.text: A lesson fee is stored as values such as `12500.00`. Which data type is most suitable?

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: Money has two decimal places and is used in calculations, so DECIMAL (or REAL) is suitable; VARCHAR would stop totals being calculated.

questions.title: Matching keys
questions.text: If `CustomerID` is VARCHAR(6) in Customer, it may be INT in Rental, because it is only a foreign key there.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: A foreign key must have the same data type and size as the primary key it refers to.

questions.title: Referential integrity
questions.text: Which statement describes **referential integrity**?

options.content: Every field must have a validation rule
Every foreign-key value must match an existing primary-key value in the linked table
Two tables may not have fields with the same name

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: E.g. a Lesson cannot refer to a student S9999 who does not exist in Student.

questions.title: Field sizes
questions.text:
Complete the data dictionary.

`StudentID` has values such as `S0107`, so its size is [[1]] characters. `ParentPhone` has values such as `+77015554433`, so its size is [[2]] characters.

scheme.explanation: Count every character, including the letter S and the + sign.

questions.title: Choose the check
questions.text: Tick (✓) the **most suitable** validation check for each field.

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 Presence (1); 2 Range (1); 3 Lookup (1); 4 Format (1)
scheme.model_answer: Surname (must be filled in) — Presence; Capacity (1 to 40 seats) — Range; Instrument (piano, dombra, violin, guitar) — Lookup; StudentID (S followed by 4 digits) — Format.
scheme.explanation: A range check needs limits; a lookup check needs a short list of allowed values; a format check needs a pattern.

questions.title: From the dictionary to SQL
questions.text: Match each data dictionary entry to the SQL that implements it.

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R4, L2–R3, L3–R2, L4–R1. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Presence check in SQL
questions.text: State the SQL keyword(s) written after a field definition so that the field **cannot be left empty**.

scheme.mark_scheme: NOT NULL
scheme.explanation: NOT NULL implements a presence check.

questions.title: Order of creating tables
questions.text: Student, Teacher and Room are each related 1:M to Lesson, which holds three foreign keys. Which table must be created **last**?

scheme.mark_scheme: D.
scheme.explanation: A foreign key can only reference a table that already exists, so the link table on the "many" side is created last.

questions.title: Complete CREATE TABLE
questions.text:
Complete the SQL.

```sql
CREATE TABLE Room (
  RoomNo   INT [[1]] KEY,
  Capacity INT [[2]] (Capacity BETWEEN 1 AND 40)
);
-- in Lesson:
FOREIGN KEY (RoomNo) [[3]] Room(RoomNo)
```

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) primary (2) check (3) references

questions.title: Errors in a data dictionary
questions.text: A data dictionary contains these rows. Select the **two** rows that contain an error.

scheme.mark_scheme: B and D. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: B: a phone number with + must be VARCHAR. D: a range check does not suit a surname — use presence / length.

questions.title: Every table has a primary key
questions.text: In a well-designed database every table, including a link table such as Lesson, has a primary key.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.
scheme.explanation: Every table needs a field (or combination of fields) that uniquely identifies each record.

questions.title: Keys in the Lesson table
questions.text: Complete the *Key* column of the data dictionary for the table `Lesson`. Write **PK**, **FK** or **none**.

scheme.mark_scheme: LessonID Key: PK (1); TeacherID Key: FK (1); LessonDate Key: none (1)
scheme.model_answer: LessonID Key: PK; TeacherID Key: FK; LessonDate Key: none
scheme.explanation: TeacherID is the primary key of Teacher, copied into Lesson to link the tables.

questions.title: Designing the Sapa sports centre database
questions.text:
The **Sapa** sports centre in Shymkent is designing a database for bookings.

*Each **member** has a member number, name, phone and date of joining. Each **coach** has a coach number, name and speciality. The centre runs fitness **classes**; each class has a class code, a title, a day, a start time and a maximum size, and is led by one coach. A member can book places on many classes, and each class is booked by many members. For every **booking** the centre records the date the booking was made and whether the member attended.*

scheme.mark_scheme: - a single property / item of data about an entity / a field (column) of a table (1)
scheme.model_answer: An attribute is one property of an entity, e.g. a member's phone number; it becomes a field of the table.

parts.title: The Member–Class relationship
parts.text: State the degree of the relationship between **Member** and **Class**, and explain how it must be implemented in the database.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- many-to-many / M:M (1)
- a field can hold only one value / a single FK cannot store many classes or many members, so it cannot be implemented directly (1)
- a link entity / table (Booking) is added with two foreign keys, giving two 1:M relationships (1)

points.criterion: Why it cannot be implemented directly
Link entity with two FKs / two 1:M

scheme.model_answer: It is M:M: a member books many classes and a class has many members. One foreign key can hold only one value, so neither table can store the link; a link table Booking with MemberNo and ClassCode as foreign keys turns it into Member 1:M Booking and Class 1:M Booking.

parts.title: Draw the ERD
parts.text: Draw the ERD for the sports centre with the entities **Member**, **Coach**, **Class** and **Booking**. Connect the related entities and give every relationship its degree. Do not leave a many-to-many relationship.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Entities: Member, Coach, Class, Booking (1 item each)
Relationships: Coach 1:M Class; Member 1:M Booking; Class 1:M Booking (1 item each, with the correct degree)
7 items; the 4 marks are given in proportion to the correct items. Each extra entity or line cancels one correct item.
scheme.model_answer: Coach 1 —— M Class; Member 1 —— M Booking; Class 1 —— M Booking

parts.title: Keys of Booking
parts.text: Identify a suitable **primary key** and the **foreign keys** of the table **Booking**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- primary key: BookingID / BookingNo (or the composite MemberNo + ClassCode) (1)
- foreign keys: MemberNo **and** ClassCode (both needed) (1)
scheme.model_answer: Primary key: BookingID. Foreign keys: MemberNo (→ Member) and ClassCode (→ Class).

questions.title: The data dictionary for Member
questions.text: The analyst at Sapa now writes the **data dictionary**. Example data for one member: member number `M0457`, name `Aliya Sarsenova`, phone `+77071234567`, date of joining `03/09/2026`.

parts.title: Data types and sizes
parts.text: Complete the data dictionary for the table **Member** by giving the most suitable **data type** and **size** of each field.

scheme.mark_scheme:
MemberNo: VARCHAR / text (5) (1)
Name: VARCHAR / text with a sensible size 30–60 (1)
Phone: VARCHAR / text, size 12 (1)
DateJoined: DATE (no size / 10) (1)
The type and the size must both be correct for the mark.
scheme.model_answer: MemberNo VARCHAR(5); Name VARCHAR(50); Phone VARCHAR(12); DateJoined DATE.

parts.title: Validation rules
parts.text: Suggest a suitable **validation rule** for each field. Give the rule, not only the name of the check.

scheme.mark_scheme:
MemberNo (1): format M followed by 4 digits / presence and unique
Phone (1): length 12 / format +7 followed by 10 digits
DateJoined (1): range, e.g. not after today / not before the centre opened; or format DD/MM/YYYY
Only the name of a check with no rule = 0.
scheme.model_answer: MemberNo: format M + 4 digits, unique. Phone: length 12, starts with +7. DateJoined: not later than today's date.

parts.title: Phone as text
parts.text: Explain why **Phone** should not be stored as an integer.

scheme.mark_scheme: - it starts with + (or 0) / contains symbols, which an integer cannot hold / would lose; no arithmetic is done with it (1)
scheme.model_answer: It begins with + and may begin with 0, which an integer cannot store, and nobody calculates with phone numbers.

parts.title: Why a data dictionary
parts.text: Explain **one** reason why the data dictionary is written **before** the tables are created.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- reason, e.g. programmers build every table with the same agreed names / types / sizes (1)
- consequence, e.g. so keys match and tables can be joined / fewer errors to fix after data is entered / validation is applied consistently (1)
scheme.model_answer: It gives programmers one agreed definition of every field, so the keys in different tables have the same type and size and the tables can be joined without rebuilding them later.

questions.title: Implementing the Booking table
questions.text:
The design of **Booking** in the data dictionary:

| Field | Type | Key | Validation |
|---|---|---|---|
| BookingID | INT, auto-increment | PK | unique |
| MemberNo | VARCHAR(5) | FK → Member | must exist in Member; presence |
| ClassCode | VARCHAR(6) | FK → Class | must exist in Class; presence |
| BookedOn | DATE | | presence |
| Attended | BOOLEAN | | default False |

parts.title: Referential integrity
parts.text: Explain the meaning of **referential integrity** using the field **MemberNo** in Booking as an example.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- every foreign-key value must match an existing primary-key value in the linked table (1)
- e.g. a booking cannot have MemberNo M9999 unless member M9999 exists in Member / a member with bookings cannot simply be deleted (1)
scheme.model_answer: Every foreign key must refer to a record that exists: a Booking can only contain a MemberNo that is already in the Member table.

parts.title: Write CREATE TABLE
parts.text: Write the SQL statement to create the table **Booking** exactly as designed, including its primary key, both foreign keys, the presence checks and the default value.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- CREATE TABLE Booking ( … ); with all five fields (1)
- suitable types matching the design, MemberNo VARCHAR(5), ClassCode VARCHAR(6), DATE, BOOLEAN (1)
- BookingID … PRIMARY KEY (1)
- FOREIGN KEY (MemberNo) REFERENCES Member(MemberNo) and FOREIGN KEY (ClassCode) REFERENCES Class(ClassCode) (1)
- NOT NULL on MemberNo, ClassCode and BookedOn, and DEFAULT FALSE on Attended (1)
Ignore minor syntax slips (capitals, commas) if the meaning is clear.
scheme.model_answer:
CREATE TABLE Booking (
  BookingID INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  MemberNo  VARCHAR(5) NOT NULL,
  ClassCode VARCHAR(6) NOT NULL,
  BookedOn  DATE NOT NULL,
  Attended  BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
  FOREIGN KEY (MemberNo)  REFERENCES Member(MemberNo),
  FOREIGN KEY (ClassCode) REFERENCES Class(ClassCode)
);

parts.title: Order of creation
parts.text: The tables Member, Coach, Class and Booking are created one by one. Explain why **Booking** must be created after Member and Class.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Booking contains foreign keys that reference Member and Class (1)
- a foreign key can only reference a table (primary key) that already exists, otherwise the statement fails (1)

points.criterion: Booking has FKs to Member and Class

scheme.model_answer: Booking's foreign keys refer to Member and Class; a foreign key can only point to a table that already exists, so those tables are created first.

parts.title: Attended
parts.text: State why **BOOLEAN** is a suitable data type for **Attended**.

scheme.mark_scheme: - it has only two possible values, true / false (yes / no) (1)
scheme.model_answer: Attendance is only yes or no, so a True/False field is enough.

questions.title: Reviewing a clinic design
questions.text:
A student designed a database for the **Densaulyq** clinic. *Each patient can have many appointments; each appointment is with one doctor; doctors have many appointments.* Part of the student's data dictionary for **Appointment**:

| Field | Type | Key | Validation |
|---|---|---|---|
| AppointmentID | INT | PK | unique |
| PatientID | INT | FK → Patient | must exist in Patient |
| DoctorName | VARCHAR(40) | | presence |
| AppDate | VARCHAR(10) | | presence |
| AppTime | TIME | | range check on the patient's surname |

In the Patient table, `PatientID` is VARCHAR(6), e.g. `P00321`.

parts.title: Errors in the design
parts.text: Identify **three** errors in this extract of the data dictionary. For each error, describe how it should be corrected.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any three errors, 1 mark for the error and 1 mark for its correction:
- PatientID is INT but the PK in Patient is VARCHAR(6) (1) → make it VARCHAR(6), the same as the PK (1)
- DoctorName stores the doctor's name in Appointment / no FK to Doctor (1) → replace it with DoctorID as a foreign key to a Doctor table (1)
- AppDate is VARCHAR (1) → use DATE so dates can be validated / sorted (1)
- AppTime validation refers to a surname / is unsuitable (1) → range check on the time, e.g. 08:00–18:00 (1)
The correction mark is only given with its error.
scheme.model_answer: 1 PatientID INT does not match VARCHAR(6) → VARCHAR(6). 2 DoctorName → DoctorID VARCHAR FK → Doctor. 3 AppDate VARCHAR → DATE (or AppTime validation → range 08:00–18:00).

parts.title: Checking a design
parts.text: Describe **two** checks the analyst should carry out on a database design **before** it is implemented.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Two checks, 1 mark for naming the check and 1 for the description:
- requirements: every report / screen the client needs can be produced from the tables (2)
- normalisation: each fact stored once / tables in 3NF / no repeated data (2)
- keys: every table has a PK and every relationship has an FK on the many side (2)
- data types and validation: each type fits the data and each field has suitable validation (2)
- test data: sample records can be entered and joined correctly (2)
scheme.model_answer: Check the design against the requirements: every report the clinic asked for, such as a doctor's daily list, can be produced from the tables. Check normalisation: each fact, such as a doctor's name, is stored only once, so the tables are in 3NF.

summary: Designing the database for a new system — finding entities and attributes in the requirements, deciding the degree of each relationship, drawing the ERD and resolving many-to-many relationships, then writing a complete data dictionary (data types, sizes, keys, validation) for every table and turning the design into CREATE TABLE statements.

theory.title: Database design in the system life cycle

blocks.content: During the **design** stage of a new system the analyst turns the **requirements specification** into an exact plan of the database. Nothing is built yet: the plan is checked with the client first, because a mistake found on paper costs minutes, but a mistake found after the tables are full of data costs days.

The stage of system design in which the analyst decides **which tables (entities)** the database will have, **which fields (attributes)** each table holds, **how the tables are related**, and the **data type, size, key and validation** of every field. Its products are the **ERD** and the **data dictionary**.
A **thing (person, object, event) about which data is stored**, with many instances — e.g. *Student*, *Teacher*, *Lesson*. Each entity becomes **one table**.
A **single property of an entity** — e.g. *Surname*, *DateOfBirth*. Each attribute becomes **one field (column)** of the table.
A **link between two entities**, e.g. *a teacher teaches many lessons*. Its **degree** is one-to-one (1:1), one-to-many (1:M) or many-to-many (M:M). In the database it is made with a **foreign key**.

A **primary key (PK)** is a field that **uniquely identifies each record** of a table (e.g. `StudentID`). A **foreign key (FK)** is a field in one table that is the **primary key of another table**, used to **link** the two tables.

blocks.caption: The steps of database design

blocks.title: The two design documents
rows: **Which tables** exist and **how they are related** (1:1, 1:M)
**Every field** of every table: name, type, size, key, validation, description, example
Second, from the entities of the ERD
Analyst and client to agree the structure
Programmers to build the tables; testers to choose test data

items.title: Why design the database first
items.content:
- Errors are found **on paper**, before data is entered.
- The client can **check** that every report they need can be produced.
- Several programmers build tables that **fit together** (same keys and types).
- The design becomes part of the **technical documentation** for maintenance.

items.title: What a good design achieves
items.content:
- Each fact is stored **once** — no data redundancy (tables in 3NF).
- Every table has a **primary key**; every relationship has a **foreign key**.
- Every field has a **suitable data type** and **validation**, so data integrity is high.
- The database can be **extended** later without rebuilding it.

theory.title: Step 1 — Entities and attributes from the requirements

blocks.content: The analyst reads the requirements and **underlines the nouns**. A noun that has **its own data** and **many instances** is an **entity**; a noun that is just **one value** about something is an **attribute**.

blocks.title: Worked example — the Aqkuy music school
blocks.content:
*The Aqkuy music school in Almaty wants a system to manage lessons. Each **student** has an ID, first name, surname, date of birth and a parent's phone number. Each **teacher** has an ID, a name and the instrument they teach. Every week a student has individual **lessons**, possibly with several different teachers; for each lesson the school records the date, the start time, the room and whether the student attended. Each **room** has a number and a capacity.*

1. **Underline the nouns:** student, ID, name, date of birth, phone, teacher, instrument, lesson, date, time, room, number, capacity.
2. **Keep the nouns with their own data and many instances:** Student, Teacher, Lesson, Room → **entities**.
3. **The other nouns describe an entity:** name, date of birth, instrument, capacity… → **attributes**.
4. **Give each entity a primary key:** StudentID, TeacherID, LessonID, RoomNo.

| Entity | Attributes (PK underlined in the ERD) |
|---|---|
| Student | **StudentID**, FirstName, Surname, DateOfBirth, ParentPhone |
| Teacher | **TeacherID**, Name, Instrument |
| Room | **RoomNo**, Capacity |
| Lesson | **LessonID**, LessonDate, StartTime, Attended (+ foreign keys added in step 2) |

blocks.title: Entity or attribute?
rows: Yes — a Teacher has an ID, a name, an instrument
No — an instrument is just one value

blocks.title: How to choose a primary key
items: Use a field that is **unique** for every record and **never empty** — e.g. a student number.
If no natural field is unique (names repeat!), **create an ID** field, often auto-incremented.
The key should **not change** over time — not a phone number or a surname.
Keep it **short** and simple, because it is copied into other tables as a foreign key.

blocks.content:
- Making a **single value** an entity — "Date" or "Instrument" are attributes, not tables.
- Choosing **Name** as a primary key — two students can have the same name.
- Forgetting the **event** entities: *Lesson*, *Loan*, *Rental*, *Order* are entities too, not only people and objects.
- Putting the same attribute (e.g. the teacher's name) into **several** entities — store it once.
For every pair of entities that are related, ask the question **in both directions**: "Can one A have many B?" and "Can one B have many A?". The two answers give the **degree** of the relationship.

blocks.title: The three degrees of relationship
rows: One A is linked to **one** B, and one B to **one** A
Teacher — Classroom they are in charge of
One A is linked to **many** B, but one B to **one** A
FK in the table on the **"many" side** (Lesson.TeacherID)
One A to **many** B **and** one B to **many** A
**Cannot be stored directly** → add a **link entity** with two FKs

blocks.title: Relationships in the music school
rows: One student has many lessons? **Yes**. One lesson is for many students? **No** (individual)
One teacher gives many lessons? **Yes**. One lesson has many teachers? **No**
One room is used for many lessons? **Yes**. One lesson uses many rooms? **No**
One student has many teachers? **Yes**. One teacher has many students? **Yes**

blocks.caption: Resolving a many-to-many relationship with a link entity

blocks.title: Drawing the ERD
items: Draw **one box per entity**, named in the singular (Student, not Students) — or plural everywhere, but be consistent.
Write the attributes in the box and mark the **PK**; add the **FKs** to the tables on the "many" side.
Join every pair of **related** entities with **one line** — not every pair is related.
Show the degree at **both ends**: `1` / single bar on the "one" side, `M` / crow's foot on the "many" side.
Label the line with a verb if it helps: *teaches*, *attends*.
Replace every **M:M** with a **link entity** that has two 1:M relationships.
Check: every table has a PK, every relationship has an FK, no fact is stored twice (3NF).

blocks.title: Worked example — resolving M:M in a school library
blocks.content:
*Members borrow many books; over a year each book is borrowed by many members.*
- Member — Book is **M:M**, so it cannot be stored directly.
- Add the link entity **Loan** (one record per borrowing) with `LoanID` (PK), `MemberID` (FK), `BookID` (FK), `LoanDate`, `ReturnDate`.
- Now **Member 1:M Loan** and **Book 1:M Loan**. The dates belong to the **Loan**, not to the member or the book — the link entity is also the right place for facts about the relationship.

- Leaving an **M:M** line in the final ERD — always resolve it with a link entity.
- Putting the foreign key on the **"one" side** (TeacherID in Teacher is a PK; the FK belongs in Lesson).
- Drawing a crow's foot at the wrong end — the crow's foot touches the entity that has **many** records per one record of the other.
- Asking the question in **one direction only** — "a student has many lessons" alone does not tell you whether it is 1:M or M:M.
- Linking every entity to every other one — draw a line only where the scenario describes a relationship.

theory.title: Exam practice: entities, relationships and the ERD

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Define the term entity. [1]**
A thing / object / person / event about which data is stored (and which becomes a table in the database) (1).

**Q: A gym records members, trainers and training sessions. Each session is for one member with one trainer. Identify the entities and the degree of each relationship. [4]**
Entities: Member, Trainer, Session (1). Member — Session **1:M** (1). Trainer — Session **1:M** (1). Member — Trainer is M:M, resolved by **Session** (the link entity) (1).

**Q: Explain why a many-to-many relationship cannot be implemented directly in a relational database. [2]**
A field can hold only **one value** (1), so neither table can hold a single foreign key for its **many** partners; a **link table** with two foreign keys is needed (1).

**Q: State where the foreign key is placed in a one-to-many relationship. [1]**
In the table on the **"many"** side (1).

**Q: Draw the ERD for: one customer places many orders; an order contains many products. [4]**
Entities Customer, Order, Product + link entity OrderLine (1); Customer 1:M Order (1); Order 1:M OrderLine (1); Product 1:M OrderLine (1).

- Writing the degree as words without saying **which entity is on the "many" side**.
- Naming the link entity vaguely ("Link", "Table3") — use a meaningful name: *Lesson*, *Loan*, *OrderLine*.
- Forgetting to give marks-worthy detail: "because it is M:M" is not an explanation — say **why** one field cannot store many values.

blocks.title: Check yourself
items: Define entity, attribute, relationship, primary key and foreign key.
From a short scenario, underline the nouns and sort them into entities and attributes.
Ask the two questions for each pair and decide 1:1, 1:M or M:M.
Draw the ERD in crow's foot notation with PKs and FKs.
Resolve an M:M relationship with a link entity and name its keys.

blocks.content: When the ERD is agreed, every entity is described **field by field** in the **data dictionary**. This is the document programmers follow to create the tables, so it must be **complete and exact**.

A document / table that describes **every field of every table** in the database — its **name, data type, size, format, key, validation rule, description** and an **example** value (data about the data — metadata).
The rule that **every foreign-key value must match an existing primary-key value** in the linked table — e.g. a Lesson cannot refer to a student `S9999` who does not exist.

blocks.title: Choosing data types and sizes
rows: Whole numbers, generated by the DBMS
Has `+`, may start with 0, no arithmetic
Allows date checks and sorting by date

blocks.title: Worked example — data dictionary for Student

blocks.caption: A foreign key must match its primary key exactly

blocks.content:
- Writing a **data type that cannot hold the example** — INT for `S0107`, INT for `+77015554433`.
- Giving a foreign key a **different type or size** from the primary key it refers to.
- Leaving the **validation** column empty for keys — a PK always needs presence + uniqueness, an FK must exist in the other table.
- A validation rule that does not suit the data — a **range** check on a surname, a **lookup** on a date of birth.
- Describing the field in the *Description* column with just its name ("StudentID — student ID"): say what it stores and why.

theory.title: Step 4 — From the design to SQL

blocks.content: In the **development** stage the data dictionary is turned line by line into `CREATE TABLE` statements: each **row** of the dictionary becomes one **field definition**, the **Key** column becomes `PRIMARY KEY` / `FOREIGN KEY … REFERENCES`, and many **validation** rules become `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`, `CHECK` and `DEFAULT`.

blocks.caption: How a data-dictionary row becomes SQL

blocks.content:
CREATE TABLE Student (
    StudentID   VARCHAR(5)  PRIMARY KEY,
    FirstName   VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    Surname     VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    DateOfBirth DATE,
    ParentPhone VARCHAR(12)
);
CREATE TABLE Teacher (
    TeacherID  VARCHAR(4)  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name       VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    Instrument VARCHAR(20)
);
CREATE TABLE Room (
    RoomNo   INT PRIMARY KEY,
    Capacity INT CHECK (Capacity BETWEEN 1 AND 40)
);
CREATE TABLE Lesson (
    LessonID   INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    StudentID  VARCHAR(5) NOT NULL,
    TeacherID  VARCHAR(4) NOT NULL,
    RoomNo     INT,
    LessonDate DATE NOT NULL,
    StartTime  TIME,
    Attended   BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
    FOREIGN KEY (StudentID) REFERENCES Student(StudentID),
    FOREIGN KEY (TeacherID) REFERENCES Teacher(TeacherID),
    FOREIGN KEY (RoomNo)    REFERENCES Room(RoomNo)
);
blocks.caption: The music school design implemented as tables

blocks.title: Data dictionary item → SQL
rows: In the form or program code (input masks, `pattern`)

blocks.content: Create the tables on the **"one" side first** (Student, Teacher, Room) and the link table (Lesson) **last** — a foreign key can only reference a table that already exists.

blocks.title: Checking the design before it is built
rows: Can every screen and report the client asked for be produced from these tables?
Is each fact stored once? No repeating groups, partial or transitive dependencies (3NF)?
Does every table have a PK? Is every relationship made with an FK on the "many" side?
Does every type fit its example? Does every field have suitable validation?
Can sample records be entered, rejected when invalid and joined correctly?

blocks.content:
- Creating the **link table first** — its foreign keys refer to tables that do not exist yet.
- A `CHECK` that contradicts the data dictionary (dictionary says 1–40, SQL says `> 0`).
- Forgetting `NOT NULL` on foreign keys that must always be filled (every lesson needs a student).

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Name four items that should be recorded in a data dictionary for each field. [4]**
Any four: field name (1), data type (1), field size / length (1), key (PK / FK) (1), validation rule, format, description, example value.

**Q: Complete the data dictionary entry for `ParentPhone`: data type, size and one validation rule. [3]**
VARCHAR / text (1); 12 (1); length check = 12 characters / format `+7` followed by 10 digits / presence (1).

**Q: Explain why `StudentID` must have the same data type and size in Student and Lesson. [2]**
It is the primary key in Student and the foreign key in Lesson, used to join the tables (1); if the types differ, values cannot be matched / stored, so the join and referential integrity fail (1).

**Q: Suggest a suitable validation rule for `StartTime` and justify it. [2]**
Range check 08:00–20:00 (1) because the school is only open in those hours, so impossible times are rejected (1).

**Q: Write the SQL to create the table `Room(RoomNo, Capacity)` with a primary key and a check that the capacity is from 1 to 40. [3]**
`CREATE TABLE Room (` with both fields and suitable types (1); `RoomNo INT PRIMARY KEY` (1); `CHECK (Capacity BETWEEN 1 AND 40)` / `CHECK (Capacity >= 1 AND Capacity <= 40)` (1).

- Giving only the **name** of a check ("range check") when the question asks for a **rule** — give the limits: "1 to 40".
- Writing "number" as a data type — use the exact type: INT, DECIMAL, VARCHAR, DATE, BOOLEAN.
- Forgetting that the size of a VARCHAR must fit the **longest** value (+7 and 10 digits = 12).
- In SQL, missing `REFERENCES Table(Field)` after `FOREIGN KEY (…)`.
